prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its main line customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains, who buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. Should Rotisserie Ranch begin selling this new product?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors in the pre-seasoned chicken market?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. Competitors freeze their chicken so they cannot pre-season it; Rotisserie Ranch has a patented sterile packaging process keeping chickens fresh for 30 days without freezing, giving it a unique advantage.

clarifying_info.q: What is Rotisserie Ranch's current market position?
clarifying_info.a: Rotisserie Ranch is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.

clarifying_info.q: How many flavors are being considered?
clarifying_info.a: Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to unsold cooked chickens?
clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers; any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out. Unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

clarifying_info.q: What is Rotisserie Ranch's competitive advantage?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so that it will remain fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary.

exhibits.title: Market Test of Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken
exhibits.shows: A price-quantity chart showing two test stores (A and B) that carried Rotisserie Ranch pre-seasoned BBQ chicken at different retail price points, with the retailer margin noted for each store.

exhibits.title: Control Group Stores
exhibits.shows: A comparison table showing weekly sales data for two control stores (Store 1 and Store 2) carrying standard rotisserie chicken alongside comparable stores carrying the store-seasoned rotisserie chicken, including retail price, seasoning cost, and retailer margin details.

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains): Will they buy pre-seasoned chicken? What are the benefits and drawbacks to grocers?
Revenue and cost implications: Does the price increase to grocers offset the cost increase to Rotisserie Ranch?
Competition: Who else offers pre-seasoned rotisserie chicken and what is their competitive position?
Market testing: How would we validate demand before a full launch?
Demand elasticity and pricing: What price point maximizes gross profit for the grocer?

questions.prompt: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; must be logically defended. YES arguments: labor cost reduction for meat department workers (no need to season in-store), economies of scale from centralized seasoning, product consistency from centralized R&D. NO arguments: loss of differentiation (grocery chains differentiate by value-added), grocers better attuned to local consumer tastes, increased inventory complexity and additional SKUs.

questions.prompt: Grocers are interested in the product but want to be sure the chickens will sell well. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market. Candidate should identify that: (1) a pilot test should be run in a subset of stores, and (2) the pilot needs a control or comparison group to isolate the effect of the new product.

questions.prompt: A test market for the BBQ chicken has been run (Exhibit 1). Should the grocers carry the product? Calculate the gross profit for each test store.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate retail margin in dollars and then gross profit for each store. Demand is linear between the two points. Candidate should recognize that Exhibit 1 alone is insufficient to answer whether grocers should switch—they need control group data to compare against the existing product. Candidate should ask for control group information (Exhibit 2).

math.setup: Retail Margin ($) = Retailer Margin % x Retail Price; Gross Profit = Margin per unit x Units sold
steps: Store A: Margin = 25% x $4.00 = $1.00 per unit; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 400 = $400
Store B: Margin = 25% x $3.00 = $0.75 per unit; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 1,000 = $750
Linear demand: slope = ($4.00 - $3.00) / (400 - 1000) = $1.00 / -600 = -$0.00167 per unit; at $3.50 midpoint: Q = 700 units
At $3.50: Margin = 25% x $3.50 = $0.875 per unit; Gross Profit = $0.875 x 700 = $612.50
math.answer: Store A gross profit = $400; Store B gross profit = $750; Optimal midpoint ($3.50) gross profit = $612.50

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 (control group), calculate the grocer variable margin and gross profit for standard rotisserie chicken, and compare to the pre-seasoned product.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute variable margin for the standard chicken using the same method, then compare directly to the pre-seasoned chicken results from Exhibit 1. Note that the gross profit increase ($100-$150 per store) represents a meaningful uplift. Candidate should also note that cannibalization is not an issue because variable margins and gross profits are identical across standard and seasoned chicken — shifting to the client's product is a net benefit either way.

math.setup: Variable Margin ($) for Rotisserie = (Retailer Margin % x Retail Price) - Seasoning Cost; Gross Profit = Margin per unit x Units sold; Units = Weekly Sales / Retail Price
steps: Store 1 Standard: Units = $1,000 / $3.33 = 300 units; Margin = 30% x $3.33 - $0.00 = $1.00/unit; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Store 2 Standard: Units = $2,000 / $2.50 = 800 units; Margin = 30% x $2.50 - $0.00 = $0.75/unit; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600
Store 1 Seasoned (comparable to test Store A): Gross Profit = $400 vs $300 standard → +$100 uplift (+33.3%)
Store 2 Seasoned (comparable to test Store B): Gross Profit = $750 vs $600 standard → +$150 uplift (+25.0%)
math.answer: Standard: Store 1 GP = $300, Store 2 GP = $600. Pre-seasoned: Store A GP = $400, Store B GP = $750. Uplift of $100-$150 per store per week. Cannibalization is not an issue as variable margins are identical.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the pre-seasoned BBQ chicken product and proceed to test the other three flavors (lemon herb, tandori, teriyaki).
Grocers can expect $100-$150 more weekly gross profit from carrying the pre-seasoned product versus their own private label — a 25-33% improvement in operating profit.

Cannibalization is not an issue: variable margins and gross profits are identical on standard and seasoned rotisserie chicken, so any shift to the client's pre-seasoned product is a net benefit for grocers.
Assuming the increased retail price to grocers offsets the increased cost of seasoning, Rotisserie Ranch will earn more money via higher volume of a higher-value product.
risks: Consumer taste risk: the four flavors may not resonate equally in all markets; continued test-and-learn needed.
Grocer adoption risk: grocers who value differentiation may resist ceding the seasoning step.
Production and supply chain risk: scaling sterile packaging to four new SKUs simultaneously adds operational complexity.
Demand forecasting risk: pre-seasoned chickens that do not sell must be thrown out at end of day, increasing waste cost.
next_steps: Run test markets for the remaining three flavors (lemon herb, tandori, teriyaki) with control groups.
Negotiate pricing with grocery chains to confirm the cost pass-through is acceptable to both parties.
Quantify potential labor savings to grocers from outsourcing the seasoning step, and use this as a selling point.
Analyze potential scale benefits to Rotisserie Ranch as pre-seasoned volume grows over time.
